questions.knowledge_point: Solving Inequalities Requiring Multiplication by a Positive Factor
questions.worked_solution:
We know that the denominator $|x|+{x}^{2}+1$ is positive for all values of $x.$ So, we can multiply both sides of the inequality by $|x|+{x}^{2}+1$ and solve the resulting inequality as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{2x+7}{|x|+{x}^{2}+1} & \ge \frac{x+4}{|x|+{x}^{2}+1} \\ (|x|+{x}^{2}+1)\cdot \frac{2x+7}{|x|+{x}^{2}+1} & \ge (|x|+{x}^{2}+1)\cdot \frac{x+4}{|x|+{x}^{2}+1} \\ 2x+7 & \ge x+4 \\ x & \ge -3 \\ x & \ge \,-3\end{aligned}
$$

questions.worked_solution:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{2{x}^{4}+3x}{{x}^{4}+2} & \le 2 \\ ({x}^{4}+2)\cdot \frac{2{x}^{4}+3x}{{x}^{4}+2} & \le ({x}^{4}+2)\cdot 2 \\ 2{x}^{4}+3x & \le 2{x}^{4}+4 \\ 3x & \le 4 \\ x & \le \frac{4}{3}\end{aligned}
$$

$$
-1\le \operatorname{sin}⁡x\le 1\,⇒\,2\le \operatorname{sin}⁡x+3\le 4.
$$

So, we can multiply both sides of the inequality by $\operatorname{sin}⁡x+3$ and solve the resulting inequality as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{9-2x}{\operatorname{sin}⁡x+3} & >\frac{x-1}{\operatorname{sin}⁡x+3} \\ (\operatorname{sin}⁡x+3)\cdot \frac{9-2x}{\operatorname{sin}⁡x+3} & >(\operatorname{sin}⁡x+3)\cdot \frac{x-1}{\operatorname{sin}⁡x+3} \\ 9-2x & >x-1 \\ -3x & >-10 \\ x & <\,\frac{10}{3}\end{aligned}
$$

questions.knowledge_point: Solving Inequalities Requiring Division by a Positive Factor
questions.worked_solution:
Since ${e}^{2x}+{x}^{4}$ is always positive, we can divide both sides of the inequality by this quantity. By doing this, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{({e}^{2x}+{x}^{4})(5x-1)}{{e}^{2x}+{x}^{4}} & <\frac{0}{{e}^{2x}+{x}^{4}} \\ 5x-1 & <0 \\ 5x & <1 \\ x & <\,\frac{1}{5}.\end{aligned}
$$

$$
-\frac{\pi }{2}<\operatorname{arctan}⁡(x+3)<\frac{\pi }{2}\,⇒\,-4\pi <2\operatorname{arctan}⁡(x+3)-3\pi <-2\pi .
$$

Since $2\operatorname{arctan}⁡(x+3)-3\pi $ is always negative, we can divide both sides of the inequality by this quantity, but we have to remember to flip the sign of the inequality. By doing this, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}(2\operatorname{arctan}⁡(x+3)-3\pi )(2x+9) & <0 \\ \frac{(2\operatorname{arctan}⁡(x+3)-3\pi )(2x+9)}{2\operatorname{arctan}⁡(x+3)-3\pi } & >\frac{0}{2\operatorname{arctan}⁡(x+3)-3\pi } \\ 2x+9 & >0 \\ 2x & >-9 \\ x & >-\frac{9}{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

$$

questions.knowledge_point: Solving Inequalities Involving Domain Restrictions
questions.worked_solution:
Since $x>2,$ we have that

$$
\begin{aligned}x & >2 \\ -x & <-2 \\ 1-x & <-1.\end{aligned}
$$

This means that $1-x$ is negative for all the values of $x$ that we are considering $(x>2).$ So, we can multiply both sides by $1-x,$ provided that we flip the sign of the inequality:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{3x+2}{1-x} & >4 \\ (1-x)\cdot \frac{3x+2}{1-x} & <(1-x)\cdot 4 \\ 3x+2 & <4-4x \\ 7x & <2 \\ x & <\frac{2}{7}\end{aligned}
$$

However, there are no numbers that satisfy both $x>2$ and $x<\frac{2}{7}.$ So, the inequality has no solution.

questions.knowledge_point: Solving Inequalities Involving Domain Restrictions
questions.worked_solution:
Since $x>3,$ we have that

$$
\begin{aligned}x & >3 \\ x-1 & >2 \\ |x-1| & >2 \\ |x-1|-1 & >1\end{aligned}
$$

This means that $|x-1|-1$ is positive for all the values of $x$ that we are considering $(x>3).$ So, we can multiply both sides by $|x-1|-1,$ and solve the resulting inequality as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{8-2x}{|x-1|-1} & \ge 0 \\ (|x-1|-1)\cdot \frac{8-2x}{|x-1|-1} & \ge (|x-1|-1)\cdot 0 \\ 8-2x & \ge 0 \\ -2x & \ge -8 \\ x & \le 4\end{aligned}
$$

Note that we had to flip the sign of the inequality again since we divided by a negative number ($-2$).

Therefore, the solution to the inequality will be the numbers that satisfy both $x>3$ and $x\le 4.$ So, the solution to our inequality is

$$
3<x\le 4.
$$

questions.knowledge_point: Solving Inequalities Involving Domain Restrictions
questions.worked_solution:
Since $x>5,$ we have that

$$
\begin{aligned}x & >5 \\ x-3 & >5-3 \\ x-3 & >2.\end{aligned}
$$

This means that $x-3$ is positive for all the values of $x$ that we are considering $(x>5).$ So, we can multiply both sides by $x-3,$ and solve the resulting inequality as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{x}{x-3} & \le 2 \\ (x-3)\cdot \frac{x}{x-3} & \le (x-3)\cdot 2 \\ x & \le 2x-6 \\ -x & \le -6 \\ x & \ge 6\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the solution to the inequality will be the numbers that satisfy both $x>5$ and $x\ge 6.$ So, the solution to our inequality is $x\ge 6.$

$$

This means that $\operatorname{ln}⁡(x-2)$ is positive for all the values of $x$ that we are considering $(x>3).$ So, we can multiply both sides by $\operatorname{ln}⁡(x-2),$ and solve the resulting inequality as follows:

\begin{aligned}\frac{2x-3}{\operatorname{ln}⁡(x-2)} & \ge 0 \\ \operatorname{ln}⁡(x-2)\cdot \frac{2x-3}{\operatorname{ln}⁡(x-2)} & \ge \operatorname{ln}⁡(x-2)\cdot 0 \\ 2x-3 & \ge 0 \\ 2x & \ge 3 \\ x & \ge \frac{3}{2}\end{aligned}

questions.worked_solution:
Since $x<-1,$ we have that

$$
\begin{aligned}x & <-1 \\ 2x & <-2 \\ 2x-1 & <-3.\end{aligned}
$$

This means that $2x-1$ is negative for all the values of $x$ that we are considering $(x<-1).$ So, we can divide both sides by $2x-1,$ provided that we flip the sign of the inequality:

$$
\begin{aligned}(2x-1)(x+3) & \ge 0 \\ \frac{(2x-1)(x+3)}{2x-1} & \le \frac{0}{2x-1} \\ x+3 & \le 0 \\ x & \le -3\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the solution to the inequality will be the numbers that satisfy both $x\le -3$ and $x<-1.$ So, the solution to our inequality is $x\le -3.$

canonical_examples.worked_solution:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{2}{5{x}^{4}+2} & <\frac{5-2x}{5{x}^{4}+2} \\ (5{x}^{4}+2)\cdot \frac{2}{5{x}^{4}+2} & <(5{x}^{4}+2)\cdot \frac{5-2x}{5{x}^{4}+2} \\ 2 & <5-2x \\ 2x & <3 \\ x & <\frac{3}{2}\end{aligned}
$$

canonical_examples.knowledge_point: Solving Inequalities Requiring Multiplication or Division by a Negative Factor
canonical_examples.worked_solution:
Note that the factor $2\sin{x}-9$ is always negative. We know this because

$$
-1 \leq \sin x \leq 1 \quad \Rightarrow \quad -11 \leq 2\sin x - 9 \leq -7.
$$

Because $2\sin{x}-9$ is always negative, we can divide both sides of the inequality by this quantity, but we have to remember to flip the sign of the inequality. By doing this, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}(2\operatorname{sin}⁡x-9)(2x) & \le 0 \\ \frac{(2\operatorname{sin}⁡x-9)(2x)}{2\operatorname{sin}⁡x-9} & \ge \frac{0}{2\operatorname{sin}⁡x-9} \\ 2x & \ge 0 \\ x & \ge 0.\end{aligned}
$$

Since $x\lt 0,$ we have that

$$
\begin{aligned}x & <0 \\ -x & >0 \\ -3x & >0 \\ 1-3x & >1.\end{aligned}
$$

This means that $1-3x$ is positive for all the values of $x$ that we are considering $(x\lt 0).$ So, we can multiply both sides by $1-3x,$ and solve the resulting inequality as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{x+5}{1-3x} & <2 \\ (1-3x)\cdot \frac{x+5}{1-3x} & <(1-3x)\cdot 2 \\ x+5 & <2-6x \\ 7x & <-3 \\ x & <-\frac{3}{7}\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the solution to the inequality will be the numbers that satisfy both $x \lt 0$ and $x \lt -\dfrac{3}{7}.$ So, the solution to our inequality is $x \lt -\dfrac{3}{7}.$
